analysis.one_liner: Bans the sale and manufacture of semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, while letting current owners keep theirs.
analysis.headline: Introduced April 30, 2025 with 42 cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and has seen no hearing or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess semiautomatic assault weapons and ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds, with a long list of named rifles, pistols, and shotguns covered [S2] [S3]. People who already legally own these weapons could keep them: grandfathered assault weapons could be sold or transferred only through a licensed dealer with a background check and must be stored securely, while grandfathered high-capacity magazines could be kept but not sold or transferred [S2]. Most hunting rifles and shotguns are exempted by name in an appendix to the bill, along with law enforcement and certain other uses [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill passed, it would be a federal crime to make, sell, transfer, or import newly defined semiautomatic assault weapons and magazines holding more than 10 rounds, aimed at reducing their availability in mass shootings and other gun violence [S2]. People in communities affected by such shootings would be the intended beneficiaries. Existing owners could keep legally owned weapons, and those weapons could only change hands through a licensed dealer with a background check [S2]. States could use existing Justice Assistance Grant funds to pay people who surrender banned weapons or magazines under a buy-back program [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition feeding devices, with exceptions for law enforcement and certain other uses.

Lets people who already legally own these weapons keep them, but requires that grandfathered assault weapons be sold or transferred only through a licensed dealer after a background check, and stored securely so people prohibited from having guns cannot reach them.
Lets state and local governments use existing Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant funds to pay people who surrender banned weapons or magazines under a buy-back program.
Requires the Attorney General to keep a public record of semiautomatic assault weapons used in crimes and report it to Congress annually.
Requires serial numbers and manufacture dates on newly made weapons and high-capacity magazines, which aids tracing.

analysis.who_pays: Current owners keep their weapons but face secure-storage rules for grandfathered assault weapons and dealer background checks before selling or transferring one [S2]. Firearms manufacturers and importers could no longer make or sell the defined weapons or new magazines holding more than 10 rounds, and dealers would lose those sales [S2] [S3]. Owners who later violate the possession or transfer rules would face criminal penalties and forfeiture of the devices [S3].

drawbacks.text: The definitions are broad: a semiautomatic rifle or pistol counts as a banned 'assault weapon' if it has even one listed feature such as a threaded barrel, barrel shroud, or a grip 'or any other characteristic that can function as a grip,' which sweeps in many ordinary semi-automatic firearms beyond the military-style rifles the debate usually centers on.

The ban covers possession, not just sale, so an existing owner who does not surrender a covered weapon or magazine through a buy-back could face criminal charges and forfeiture, even though the weapons were bought legally.

Compliance depends heavily on voluntary buy-backs funded through existing grant money, and grandfathered weapons stay in circulation for decades, so the bill's practical effect on gun violence would depend on how many owners give up their weapons.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is fewer military-style semiautomatic rifles and high-capacity magazines available for purchase, which supporters argue would reduce deaths in mass shootings. The cost falls on gun owners, who face storage mandates, background-checked transfers, and criminal exposure for possession if they do not surrender covered items, and on a firearms industry that would lose a product line. An honest weighing also has to acknowledge that the bill's effect depends on contested empirical ground: the earlier 1994 federal ban expired after a decade, and researchers have generally found its measurable effect on overall gun violence was modest, so the bill's public-safety payoff is uncertain while its restrictions on a large class of commonly owned firearms are definite. The breadth of the feature-based definitions is a genuine design weakness, though the appendix exempting most hunting and sporting guns narrows the practical reach.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, and the record shows no hearing, vote, or further action since.

narrative.text: Sen. Adam Schiff introduced the bill on April 30, 2025, with 42 cosponsors, all Democrats or the independent who caucuses with them.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day; the action history shows no hearing, markup, or vote since.

The bill defines the banned weapons both by features (such as a pistol grip, folding stock, threaded barrel, or barrel shroud on a semiautomatic rifle) and by a long list of named models including AR and AK types.

The bill grandfathers weapons and magazines already legally owned, requires secure storage of grandfathered assault weapons, and requires a licensed dealer background check before a private sale or transfer of one.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far no one has gained or lost anything concrete, because the bill has not advanced. Opponents of a federal assault weapons ban are better off as long as it sits without a hearing, since an unacted-on bill cannot become law.

for.name: Sen. Adam Schiff
for.role: U.S. Senator from California, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 42 cosponsors on the day of introduction.

for.name: Senate Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors, including the Senate party leader, giving the bill its full Democratic caucus-level sponsorship.

against.name: National Rifle Association and allied gun-rights groups
against.what_they_did: Has long campaigned against federal bans on semiautomatic rifles and magazines, and the bill attracted no Republican cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: All 42 cosponsors are Democrats or the independent who caucuses with Democrats, and no Republican signed on, so support runs entirely down one side of the aisle.

industries.note: Manufacturers and importers would be barred from making or selling the defined semiautomatic rifles, pistols, and shotguns and new magazines over 10 rounds, cutting off a segment of their market. Existing inventory of grandfathered weapons could still be sold through dealers.

Sales of newly banned models would end, and private transfers of grandfathered assault weapons would have to run through a licensed dealer with a background check, adding cost and friction to those transactions.

Most hunting and sporting firearms are either excluded because they are manually operated or rimfire, or listed by name in the bill's Appendix A of exempted firearms, so their core market stays legal.

analysis.trajectory: With the 119th Congress still in session, the bill sits at the earliest stage: referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee with no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled. A bill with no Republican cosponsors would typically need the committee's majority-party leadership to schedule it, and without that it would most likely sit in committee for the rest of the Congress, as similar bills in past Congresses have.
